issues.legal_issue: A tenant who omits an available statutory tenancy defense in an earlier eviction proceeding may be barred from raising it later to require a reference to a specialist tribunal.
material_facts: The landlords first sought eviction in rent-control proceedings. The tenant denied their title but did not raise the statutory protection he later claimed for a commercial lease or seek a reference on that basis.

The tenant separately sought assignment of the land under the land-reform statute on the basis of agricultural tenancy. The Land Tribunal rejected that claim after finding that the lease concerned a commercial building, not agricultural land.
The landlords later brought a civil eviction suit. The tenant then claimed protection for a commercial lease and argued that the civil court had to refer the tenancy issue to the Land Tribunal.
The Court treated the later statutory defense as one that could and ought to have been raised in the earlier eviction proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The tenant could not later rely on the omitted statutory defense to require a reference to the Land Tribunal or to challenge the civil court’s jurisdiction. The High Court’s rejection of the claim was upheld and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Explanation IV to Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a matter that might and ought to have been raised as a ground of defence in an earlier proceeding is treated as having been directly and substantially in issue; its omission can therefore operate as constructive res judicata and waiver. The Court applied that principle to the tenant’s claim under Section 106 and proposed reference under Section 125(3) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, in the context of the earlier eviction proceedings under Section 11 of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act. It approved Narayanan v. Kunchi Amma Parukutty Ammal. It distinguished Abdulrahiman v. Abdulla Haji, which had not decided the res judicata issue. The Court also observed that pursuing a claim under Section 72-B while omitting the distinct Section 106 protection did not permit the tenant to raise that omitted protection later, and that successive omission of available pleas can abuse the process and cause multiplicity of proceedings.

rule.if: earlier_eviction_proceeding and later_eviction_proceeding and same_parties and omitted_available_tenancy_defense and later_tribunal_referral_claim

predicates.earlier_eviction_proceeding: A landlord first pursued eviction of a tenant in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.later_eviction_proceeding: The landlord later pursued eviction of the same tenant in a subsequent proceeding.
predicates.same_parties: The earlier and later proceedings involved the same opposing parties or persons claiming through them.
predicates.omitted_available_tenancy_defense: The tenant could and ought to have raised a statutory tenancy defense in the earlier proceeding but did not raise it.
predicates.later_tribunal_referral_claim: In the later proceeding, the tenant relied on that defense to claim that the matter had to be referred to a specialist tribunal.

issues.definition: When the same parties pursue successive eviction proceedings and the tenant omits an available tenancy defense in the earlier proceeding but later uses it to seek a tribunal referral, the later tenancy defense is barred.
